extracted.intended_audience: General readers interested in Texas legislation, educators, librarians, legal observers
extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia encyclopedia entry summarizing Texas Senate Bill 412: its purpose, textual change to the Penal Code, legislative history, effective date, and criticism. The page explains who is affected and references obscenity law (Miller v. California).

rubrics_metrics.name: Removal of affirmative defense protections for educators
rubrics_metrics.description: "Texas Senate Bill 412 is a law that removes the affirmative defense protection from the Texas Penal Code relating to sharing and making available educational materials to minors."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The bill's language amends the Penal Code to remove the affirmative defense clause for potentially "harmful material" in educational or library settings; it specifically targets protections previously available to state educators. Legislative history: passed Texas Senate March 19, 2025; passed Texas House early May (92–39); signed by Governor Greg Abbott May 19, 2025; went into effect September 1, 2025. The page notes the change also affects parents, medical professionals, and public libraries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendment to 'Sale, Distribution or Display of Harmful Material to Minors' section
rubrics_metrics.description: "The language of the bill amends the Texas Penal Code regarding the 'Sale, Distribution or Display of Harmful Material to Minors' by removing the affirmative defense clause regarding potentially 'harmful material' in educational or library settings."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This identifies the specific statutory section altered by SB 412 — the statutory regime regulating sale, distribution, or display of material to minors — and clarifies that the statutory affirmative defense for certain actors in educational/library contexts was removed. The page does not reproduce the statutory text but links the amendment to that named section.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obscenity standard — Miller v. California three-prong test
rubrics_metrics.description: "This section of the penal code was written after the 1973 Supreme Court of the United States decided on Miller v. California and created a three-prong test for obscenity."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes that SB 412 does not itself redefine what is "harmful or inappropriate for minors"; those substantive definitions remain tied to the obscenity framework established in Miller v. California (the referenced "three-prong test"). The page does not list the three prongs verbatim but links the penal-code standard to the Miller obscenity test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-amendment of definitions of 'harmful' or 'inappropriate' material
rubrics_metrics.description: SB 412 "does not amend the Texas Penal Code in the section on what is considered harmful or inappropriate for minors."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although SB 412 removes the affirmative defense clause, it leaves intact the existing statutory/constitutional standards that define harmful or obscene material (as informed by Miller). Thus, the legal threshold for labeling material 'harmful' remains governed by the preexisting law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critics' evaluative concern: chilling effect and encouragement of book banning
rubrics_metrics.description: The ACLU describes the law as "encouraging book banning" by creating a "chilling effect" on educators, librarians, medical professionals and parents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article records critical evaluations as a metric for assessing the law's impact: whether the law discourages educators and librarians from providing or discussing materials with minors. Critics give examples of books that could be affected, citing any book with "elements of sexuality" (the article names the Bible, Brave New World, and The Scarlet Letter as illustrative examples).
